title: Chapter Tests for Class 12 Mathematics: How to Use Them (with CBSE Weightage) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Chapter Tests Class 12 Mathematics + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Why chapter tests beat re-doing exercises for Class 12 Maths, how to use them chapter by chapter with CBSE weightage, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: You can finish every NCERT exercise and still freeze in the exam hall. The fix is not more reading — it is timed chapter tests. Here is how to use them chapter by chapter, with the CBSE weightage that tells you where to spend your hours.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a scene I have watched too many times. A Class 12 student has solved every NCERT exercise in Calculus, twice, and can recite the steps for integration by parts on demand. Then the board paper puts a definite integral inside a word problem, gives 90 minutes for four questions like it, and the student stares at the page. The maths was never the issue. The exam was. This is exactly the gap that chapter tests for Class 12 Mathematics are built to close — and why finishing the textbook is not the same as being ready.

A chapter test is a short, timed paper on one chapter, taken under exam-like conditions and then marked honestly. It is not revision. It is rehearsal. Below is how I use them with students, in the order that actually moves marks.

Why chapter tests beat re-doing exercises

Re-reading a solved example feels productive because it feels easy. That ease is the trap. Your brain recognises the worked steps and mistakes recognition for recall — a well-documented illusion in learning research. A chapter test forces the opposite: you pull the method out of memory cold, with no worked example in front of you. That act of retrieval is what builds a memory strong enough to survive exam stress.

There is a second thing tests train that exercises never touch: temperament. Exam nerves, the ticking clock, deciding when to abandon a question you are stuck on and move on — these are skills, and the only way to practise them is under a timer. A student who has sat ten timed chapter tests before the boards walks in having already felt that pressure. It is old news by then.

Start with the CBSE weightage, not chapter one

Not every chapter deserves equal time. The CBSE Class 12 Maths paper is 80 marks, and the marks are far from evenly spread. Before you test anything, look at where the marks actually live:

UnitMarks (out of 80)
Calculus35
Vectors & 3-D Geometry14
Algebra (Matrices & Determinants)10
Relations & Functions8
Probability8
Linear Programming5

Calculus alone is nearly 44% of the paper. If your chapter tests give equal weight to Linear Programming and Calculus, you have your priorities backwards. Test the heavy units first, test them most often, and do not let the short chapters — which are also the easiest to master — steal time from the ones that decide your rank.

A chapter-by-chapter routine that works

The sequence matters. Here is the rhythm I recommend once you have finished learning a chapter:

  • Learn, then wait. Do not test a chapter the same day you finish it. Give it a day. A test after a gap reveals what genuinely stuck, not what is fresh in short-term memory.
  • Test cold, with a timer. Sit the chapter test in one go — roughly one minute per mark — with no notes, no phone, no peeking. Treat it as the real thing.
  • Mark it against a solution key. Be strict. In the boards you lose method marks for skipped steps, so mark yourself the way an examiner would, not the way a kind friend would.
  • Re-test after a week. The chapters you scored worst on go back into the queue. A single test tells you where you stand; a second test a week later tells you whether you fixed it.

For a heavy unit like Calculus, break it down — a separate test for Continuity and Differentiability, for Application of Derivatives, for Integrals, for Differential Equations. One giant Calculus test hides which sub-topic is leaking marks. Four focused ones point straight at it.

How to analyse a test — the step most students skip

Taking the test is the easy half. The marks are made in the analysis, and this is where most students quit too early. Do not just note the score and move on. For every question you got wrong or left blank, sort it into one of three buckets:

  • Concept gap — you did not know the method. Go back to that topic and relearn it before you test again.
  • Silly slip — a sign error, a dropped constant of integration, a misread ±. These cost more marks than students admit. Keep a running ‘error log’ in the back of a notebook; patterns show up fast.
  • Time trap — you knew it but ran out of time. This is a strategy problem, not a knowledge one, and the fix is deciding in advance how many minutes each question gets.

In my experience, a Tier-2 city student who keeps an honest error log for a month gains more marks from cutting silly slips than from learning any new topic. The concept gaps are obvious; the recurring − sign that costs you two marks in every integral is the silent killer.

A realistic weekly plan

Do not attempt a full mock paper every week — it is exhausting and it blurs which chapter is weak. A saner rhythm during the year: two chapter tests a week on the units you are currently studying, one re-test of an older weak chapter, and a full 80-mark mock only in the final six to eight weeks before the boards. That last stage is where you stitch the chapters together and practise pacing across the whole three hours. Chapter tests build the parts; mocks assemble the machine.

One honest caveat: chapter tests will feel harder than re-reading, and your early scores may sting. That discomfort is the point. A 60% on a cold timed test is worth more to you than a comfortable 100% on an exercise you have already seen the answers to.

Test yourself right now

Below is a free 8-question quiz drawn from across the Class 12 syllabus — matrices, calculus, vectors, probability and more — so you can feel what cold retrieval is like before you commit to a full chapter test. Try it, then read the explanations for anything you miss. When you are ready for proper timed practice, the chapter-test e-book at the end gives full papers with worked solution keys, one chapter at a time.

quiz.title: Class 12 Maths Chapter Test Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions from across the Class 12 syllabus — matrices, calculus, vectors, probability and LPP. Answer each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is the order of the matrix having 2 rows and 3 columns?
questions.explanation: Order is written as (rows) × (columns), so a matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns is of order 2 × 3.

questions.q: If A is a 3 × 3 matrix with |A| = 5, then |2A| equals:
questions.explanation: For an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|. Here |2A| = 2³ × 5 = 8 × 5 = 40.

questions.q: The derivative of tan x with respect to x is:
questions.explanation: d/dx (tan x) = sec² x. This is a standard result you should recall instantly.
∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C. The modulus matters because x can be negative.

questions.q: The value of the definite integral ∫₀^(π/2) cos x dx is:
questions.explanation: ∫ cos x dx = sin x, so the value is sin(π/2) − sin 0 = 1 − 0 = 1.

questions.q: If two vectors a and b satisfy a · b = 0, then the vectors are:
questions.explanation: The dot product is zero exactly when the angle between the vectors is 90°, so they are perpendicular.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is:
questions.explanation: Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, so P = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.q: In a linear programming problem, the optimal value of the objective function occurs at:
options: the centre of the feasible region
a corner point of the feasible region
questions.explanation: By the corner-point theorem, the maximum or minimum of the objective function is attained at a vertex (corner point) of the feasible region.

faq.q: How are chapter tests different from just solving NCERT exercises?
faq.a: An NCERT exercise is untimed and open-book — you can flip back to the example. A chapter test is timed, closed-book and marked strictly, so it trains recall and exam temperament, not just the method. Both matter, but only tests rehearse the exam.

faq.q: How many chapter tests should I take before the CBSE boards?
faq.a: Aim for at least one timed test per chapter, and two or three for the heavy units in Calculus. Space them out, re-test your weak chapters, and save full 80-mark mocks for the final six to eight weeks.

faq.q: Which Class 12 Maths chapters carry the most marks?
faq.a: Calculus dominates at 35 of 80 marks, followed by Vectors and 3-D Geometry at 14, and Algebra (Matrices and Determinants) at 10. Test the heavy units first and most often.

faq.q: What should I do after scoring a chapter test?
faq.a: Sort every wrong answer into concept gaps, silly slips, or time traps. Relearn the concept gaps, keep an error log for the slips, and set per-question time limits for the traps. The analysis is where the marks are actually made.
